16350: To trounce someone means to defeat them completely, decisively, and by a very large margin. It is not just winning — it is winning so overwhelmingly that the other side looks almost helpless. Think of a football match that ends 9–0. The winning team didn't just beat the other team. They trounced them.

This is what separates "trounce" from a plain word like "beat" or "defeat." When you trounce someone, the gap between the winner and the loser is huge and obvious. The winner looks dominant; the loser looks outclassed. There is a sense of complete, one-sided domination packed into this single word — almost as if the result was never in doubt.

It also carries a punchy, vivid energy. When a journalist writes "Team A trounced Team B," they are not just reporting a result — they are making you feel how lopsided it was.

Trounce works in any situation where two sides compete and one side wins so convincingly that the other is left far behind.

Sports and games — "India trounced Australia by 200 runs." / "She trounced her chess opponent in just 12 moves."

Politics and elections — "The incumbent senator trounced his rival, winning by 40 percentage points."

Competitions and contests — "He trounced every other debater in the tournament."

Business — "Our company trounced the competition this quarter, capturing 60% of the market."
How It Differs from Similar Words

This is where the real precision of "trounce" lives.

Beat / Defeat — These are neutral. They simply mean you won, with no clue about how close or one-sided it was. "She beat him" could mean she won by one point or a hundred.

Trounce — Tells you immediately that the victory was massive and lopsided. Not even close.

Thrash — Almost identical in meaning to trounce. Both imply a heavy defeat. "Thrash" can sometimes sound slightly more aggressive or physical in tone, but in sports contexts they are nearly interchangeable.

Crush — Also implies dominance, but "crush" has a slightly more violent, intense feel and is used more broadly. You can "crush someone's dreams" — but you cannot "trounce someone's dreams." Trounce is strictly about competitive defeat.

Edge out / Narrowly beat — These are the opposite of trounce. They signal a very close, tight win.

The key test: If the margin of victory was thin, uncertain, or hard-fought, you cannot use trounce. Trounce always requires a convincing, dominant, runaway victory. Using it for a close result would be inaccurate and would confuse your reader.

In older English, "trounce" also meant to beat someone physically — to thrash them with blows. This meaning is now rare and largely outdated. In modern everyday use, you will almost never encounter it with this physical sense. Stick to the competitive/defeat meaning in your own usage.

Trounce is informal to moderately informal. It is extremely common in sports journalism, news headlines, and casual conversation about competitions. Writers reach for it specifically because it is more vivid and expressive than the plain word "defeated." You would not typically use it in formal academic writing, but it fits naturally in newspapers, sports commentary, and everyday speech.

Here is a range of examples so the word becomes fully real to you:

  • The home team trounced their rivals 7–0 in front of a stunned crowd.
  • At the science fair, her project trounced all the others and took first place with ease.
  • In the spelling bee, he trounced his competitors by correctly spelling every word while others stumbled on the third round.
  • The challenger trounced the reigning chess champion, winning five games in a row without a single loss.
  • Our debate team trounced every opponent at the national competition, leaving the judges with little to deliberate.
One-Line Summary to Lock It In
Trounce = to defeat someone completely and by a very large margin, making the result feel utterly one-sided and dominant — far beyond a simple win.
16351:
A troupe is a group of performers — such as actors, dancers, acrobats, circus artists, or comedians — who work together as an organized unit, usually in a professional or semi-professional setting.

Two things define a troupe absolutely:

The members must be performers — people whose craft involves entertaining an audience. A random group of friends is not a troupe. A group of office workers is not a troupe. But a group of ballet dancers who rehearse and perform together? That is a troupe.

It must be a group — never a single person. You would say "a troupe of actors," never "a troupe of one actor."
What kinds of performers form a troupe?

The word is used most commonly for theater companies, dance groups, circus performers, acrobatic teams, comedy groups, and puppet shows. You'll hear phrases like "a theatre troupe," "a dance troupe," "a circus troupe," or "an improv comedy troupe" regularly.

Historically, troupes were traveling groups. They would move from town to town — sometimes on wagons, later on trains — and perform wherever they could find an audience. This history gives the word a certain flavor: a sense of a tight-knit, road-tested, close community of artists who have been through things together. Even in modern usage, the word carries that warmth. However, a troupe does not have to travel today. A resident theater company that performs in one fixed city is still called a troupe.

• "A troupe of dancers took the stage at midnight."
  • "The circus troupe had been performing together for over a decade."
  • "She auditioned for a local acting troupe and got the part."
  • "The comedy troupe made the entire audience roar with laughter."
Troupe vs. Troop — a very common mix-up

These two words sound completely identical when spoken, so they get confused in writing constantly. Here's how to keep them apart:

Troop refers to a group of soldiers, a group of Boy Scouts or Girl Scouts, or loosely, any assembled crowd of people. It can also refer to a group of certain animals — a troop of baboons, for instance.

Troupe refers only and specifically to a group of performers.

A simple trick: if there's a stage, a spotlight, or a curtain involved — write troupe. If there are uniforms, weapons, or merit badges — write troop.

A trouper is a member of a troupe. But this word has grown beyond its literal meaning and is now used widely in everyday English to mean someone who is reliable, hardworking, cheerful under pressure, and never complains — even in difficult circumstances. This comes from the image of a veteran performer who keeps going through exhaustion, a bad crowd, or a broken stage. The show must go on, and a trouper makes sure it does.

Example: "She stayed late every night to finish the project without a single grumble. She's a real trouper."

Be careful: trouper (performer / reliable person) is different from trooper (a soldier or a state police officer). They sound the same but mean different things.

Think of a troupe as a performing family — a close-knit group of people who share a craft, depend on each other, and bring their art to an audience together. The word carries warmth and artistry that a plain word like "group" or "team" simply doesn't. When you call a set of performers a troupe, you're suggesting they are serious about what they do, function as a cohesive unit, and share a common identity. It's a word that respects the people it describes.
16352:
A trousseau is the personal collection of clothes, linens, and other belongings that a bride puts together before her wedding — specifically to take with her into her new married life and new home.

Think of it as a bride's "starter pack" for her life after marriage: everything she'll need once she crosses the threshold of her new household.

Traditionally, a trousseau had two broad categories of items:

Personal clothing and intimate wear — nightgowns, undergarments, lingerie, daywear, formal dresses, accessories, shoes. These are things the bride will use personally, day to day.

Household linens and domestic items — bedsheets, pillowcases, tablecloths, napkins, towels, embroidered handkerchiefs. These are things she'll use to run her new home.

The defining quality of a trousseau is that every item is hers. She brings it in; it isn't purchased after the wedding or shared ownership from day one.

Historically, when a woman married, she physically moved out of her family's home and into her husband's household. She was essentially starting fresh in a place that had nothing of her own.

The trousseau was her family's way of ensuring she arrived prepared. Families — especially mothers — spent years collecting and stitching items for their daughters' trousseaux. Some families began as early as when the girl was a child. Items were often handmade with great care: hand-embroidered monograms on linens, hand-stitched nightgowns, lovingly folded and stored in cedar-lined chests.

A well-stocked trousseau was also a source of pride. In many cultures, it was displayed for guests and family before or during the wedding, almost like an exhibition. The abundance and quality of a bride's trousseau spoke to her family's prosperity, care, and status.
Is a trousseau the same as a dowry?

No — and this is a distinction worth knowing clearly.

A dowry is money, land, or property that a bride's family transfers to the groom or his family at the time of marriage. It was a financial transaction between families.

A trousseau, on the other hand, stays with the bride — personally. It belongs to her. It is her clothing and her linens, not a payment or transfer of wealth to anyone else. The trousseau moves with her into the marriage; she doesn't hand it over to anyone.
How is the word typically used?

You'll mostly encounter trousseau in the context of weddings and bridal traditions.

  • "She spent months assembling her trousseau before the wedding."
  • "The trousseau chest was passed down through the family."
  • "Her trousseau included twelve sets of embroidered bedsheets."

Occasionally, in modern usage, the word is used more narrowly to mean just the bridal lingerie and intimate sleepwear — the most personal layer of what a bride brings into the marriage. This narrower meaning has become more common as the broader domestic tradition has faded.
Is this tradition still alive today?

The full, elaborate trousseau as a formal tradition is largely a thing of the past in most Western cultures. The reasons are straightforward: women today are financially independent, often already have their own homes before marriage, and don't need to "arrive equipped" in the old-fashioned sense.

However, the concept hasn't entirely disappeared. Many brides still shop for new lingerie, nightwear, and special clothing before their wedding — sometimes called a trousseau informally, even if it's just a few selected items rather than a chest full of handmade linens.

In many South Asian, Middle Eastern, and Mediterranean cultures, some version of this tradition remains genuinely alive, with families still lovingly preparing collections of clothing and household goods for daughters before their weddings.

A trousseau is a bride's personally assembled collection of clothing, linens, and domestic belongings — gathered before marriage and carried into her new life and new home. It was historically a cherished, carefully prepared expression of readiness for married life, rooted in a time when a woman's move into her husband's household was a true beginning from scratch. The word today most often surfaces in historical, literary, or cultural contexts, or in the narrower modern sense of a bride's intimate and personal wardrobe for her new life.
16353:
A trout is a type of fish. More specifically, it is a freshwater fish — meaning it lives in rivers, streams, and lakes (not the sea), though a few types can spend time in saltwater too.

Trout belong to the salmon family, which means they are close relatives of salmon. They share many qualities: a streamlined, torpedo-shaped body built for swimming in fast-moving water, and a similar life cycle in some cases.

Trout are medium-sized fish, typically anywhere from 20 cm to over 90 cm long, depending on the species and how well-fed they are. They have:

  • A sleek, smooth body tapering at both ends
  • Spots or speckles on their body — often black, red, or orange dots, sometimes with a halo around them
  • A small, fleshy extra fin on the back near the tail (called an adipose fin — a feature shared with salmon and a few other related fish)
  • Firm, slightly oily flesh that ranges from white to pink to deep orange-red in color depending on diet

They are generally considered beautiful fish, prized for their vivid patterns.

The most important thing to understand about trout is that they are demanding about their environment. They need:

  • Cold water — most species thrive between 10°C and 16°C. Warmer temperatures stress or kill them.
  • Clean, clear water — they cannot survive in polluted or murky water.
  • Well-oxygenated water — fast-flowing streams and rivers are ideal because moving water picks up oxygen from the air.

Because of this, trout are often used as an indicator species — if trout are living in a river, the water is clean and healthy. If they disappear, something is wrong with the ecosystem.

They are found naturally across North America, Europe, and parts of Asia, but have been introduced to rivers and lakes all over the world (including South America, New Zealand, South Africa, and India) for sport fishing.

Trout are carnivores (meat eaters). They are active hunters and eat:

  • Insects — both aquatic insects (such as mayflies, caddisflies, and stoneflies, often as larvae under water) and flying insects that fall onto the water's surface
  • Worms and small invertebrates
  • Small fish — larger trout will readily eat smaller fish, including younger trout
  • Crustaceans (such as freshwater shrimp) and sometimes frogs or small amphibians

Trout have sharp eyesight and are known to be cautious and intelligent for a fish, which is part of why catching them is considered a skill.

There are many species of trout. The most commonly known ones are:

Rainbow trout — Probably the most well-known in the world. It has a distinctive pink or reddish stripe running along its side, with black spots on a silver or greenish body. Originally native to the western coast of North America, it has been introduced globally. It is also the most widely farmed trout and the most common trout you'll find in a supermarket or restaurant.

Brown trout — Native to Europe and western Asia. It has a golden-brown to olive body covered in dark spots, often with reddish or orange spots surrounded by pale rings. It is known for being particularly wary and difficult to catch.

Brook trout — Native to eastern North America. It is often considered one of the most beautiful freshwater fish, with a stunning pattern of red dots surrounded by blue halos on its sides, and vivid orange-red fins edged with black and white. Despite being called a "trout," it is technically a char (a close relative within the salmon family).

Lake trout — A large species found in deep, cold lakes in North America. It can grow very big, sometimes exceeding 10 kg.

Cutthroat trout — Native to western North America, named for the distinctive red or orange slash marks on either side of the jaw, as if the throat has been cut.

Sea trout — Not a separate species but a form of the brown trout that migrates to the sea and returns to freshwater to breed, similar to how salmon behave.

Trout has been eaten by humans for thousands of years and remains a popular food today. It is widely regarded as:

  • Delicious and nutritious — it is rich in protein and omega-3 fatty acids (healthy fats)
  • Versatile in the kitchen — it can be baked, pan-fried, grilled, smoked, or poached
  • Milder than salmon — people who find salmon too rich or oily often prefer trout

Rainbow trout is the species most commonly farmed and sold in markets. Smoked trout is a particularly popular delicacy in Europe.

Trout are one of the most celebrated sport fish (fish that are fished for the thrill of catching, not just for food) in the world. Fly fishing — a technique where a lightweight artificial lure called a "fly" is cast onto the water to mimic an insect — was essentially developed around trout fishing. It is considered an art form and has a long, rich cultural tradition, especially in Britain and North America.

Trout fishing requires patience, skill, and an understanding of the fish's behaviour. Catching a large, wild trout in a cold mountain stream is considered one of the great experiences in angling (the hobby of fishing with a rod and line).

In many countries, trout rivers and streams are carefully managed, with rules about fishing seasons, minimum sizes, and limits on how many fish you can keep, in order to protect the population.

The plural of trout follows an interesting rule:

  • When you are talking about more than one fish of the same species, the plural is simply "trout" (no change). For example: "I caught five trout today." This is similar to how "fish" is used as its own plural.
  • When you are talking about multiple different species together, you can say "trouts." For example: "The river holds rainbow trouts, brown trouts, and brook trouts." However, this usage is less common in everyday speech.

In practice, "trout" (unchanged) is the form you will encounter most of the time.

In British English, "trout" is also used informally — and somewhat unkindly — to describe a bad-tempered, unpleasant, or foolish old woman. It is usually phrased as "old trout." For example: "Don't be such an old trout." This usage is old-fashioned and not particularly common today, but you may come across it in older British literature or television. It has nothing to do with the fish itself — the connection is unclear — and is simply an insult rooted in British slang.

A trout is a beautiful, spotted, cold-water fish closely related to salmon, valued both as a food and as a prized catch for sport fishermen. It needs exceptionally clean, cold, oxygen-rich freshwater to survive, and its presence in a river is a sign of a healthy ecosystem. There are many species — rainbow, brown, brook, lake, cutthroat being the most notable — each with its own distinctive look and home range. It is delicious to eat, rich in healthy fats, and central to the tradition of fly fishing. And, rarely, in older British speech, it is also a mildly rude word for a grumpy old woman.
16354:
A trove is a rich, impressive collection of things that are considered valuable, interesting, or useful — especially one that has been found or uncovered. Think of it as a rewarding discovery of many good things gathered in one place.

The word almost always implies three things at once: abundance (there's a lot of it), value (the things matter — they're worth something, whether in money, knowledge, or interest), and discovery (it was found, revealed, or stumbled upon, rather than something ordinary and expected).

Imagine an old house being demolished. Workers dig up the floor and find hundreds of ancient gold coins buried underneath. That collection of coins is a trove. Now notice what makes it a trove and not just a "collection" or a "pile": it was discovered, it's large, and it's genuinely valuable.

But here's what makes "trove" a powerful and flexible word — the "value" doesn't have to be money. Consider these:

  • A historian discovers a forgotten box of letters written by Abraham Lincoln. That box is a trove of historical documents.
  • A researcher finds a database full of rare, unpublished scientific data. That database is a trove of information.
  • A book lover walks into an old, dusty shop and finds hundreds of rare first-edition books. The shop is a trove of rare books.

In every case, the thing being called a trove is abundant, genuinely valuable (in whatever way matters to the person or situation), and has a feeling of being discovered or revealed.

"Trove" is not a neutral word. It carries a sense of excitement, delight, and pleasant surprise — the feeling you get when you find something far better and richer than you expected. When someone calls something a trove, they are expressing that finding it felt like striking gold.

This is why you'll often see it paired with words like rich, vast, absolute, or veritable — as in "a rich trove of data" or "a veritable trove of secrets" — because writers reach for "trove" when they want to convey that a discovery is impressive and exciting, not just large.

A trove can refer to something physically real, like a collection of buried artifacts, antique jewels, or old manuscripts stored in an attic. These are tangible things you can hold.

But "trove" is equally — and in modern usage, perhaps even more — commonly used for abstract things: a trove of information, a trove of memories, a trove of ideas, a trove of research. As long as the collection is rich, valuable in some sense, and feels like a discovery, calling it a trove is perfectly natural.

You will very often see the phrase treasure trove, which is the older and more traditional form. "Treasure trove" historically referred specifically to gold, silver, or valuables found hidden in the ground with no known owner (it was even a legal term). Over time, people began using "treasure trove" more loosely to mean any surprisingly rich discovery of valuable things. Eventually, "trove" broke free and began standing on its own, carrying the same meaning — a rich, discovered collection of valuable things — without needing "treasure" attached to it. Both forms are widely used today, and both mean essentially the same thing in everyday language.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Collection is simply a group of things brought together. It says nothing about whether those things are valuable or how they were found. A trove is always a remarkable collection — one that impresses you.

Hoard refers to a store of things that someone has secretly gathered and hidden, often suggesting selfishness or secrecy (people "hoard" food, money, or supplies). A trove, on the other hand, is what someone discovers — it's the exciting find, not the selfish hiding. The two words are often related in situation (you might find a trove where someone once had a hoard), but the tone is very different.

Cache means a hidden store of things. It's more neutral and often used in practical or military contexts (a cache of weapons, a cache of supplies). A cache becomes a trove when the person who finds it is impressed by how valuable or rich it is.

Stash is informal and similar to cache — a hidden supply of something. Like "hoard," it focuses on the hiding, while "trove" focuses on the thrilling discovery.

If you want to use "trove" correctly and naturally, think of it this way: whenever you discover — or want to describe discovering — a surprisingly large and valuable collection of things (physical or abstract), and that discovery feels exciting, the word "trove" fits perfectly.

A single rare coin is not a trove. One interesting document is not a trove. But hundreds of rare coins buried under centuries of soil? A massive archive of never-before-seen letters from a famous writer? A hard drive containing thousands of previously unknown photographs? Those are troves — rich, impressive, exciting discoveries of many valuable things at once.
16355: A trowel is a small, handheld tool made up of two basic parts: a flat or scooped blade (usually metal) and a short handle attached to it. You hold it in one hand and use the blade to either spread a material onto a surface or dig into the ground. That's the core idea — a tool you grip in one hand to do work with its blade.

The word "trowel" refers to two distinct tools that look somewhat different and are used in completely different situations. Both go by the same name because they share the same basic form: a blade + a handle.

1. The Masonry Trowel (or Bricklayer's Trowel)

This is the trowel used in construction work — by bricklayers, plasterers, and tile setters.

What it looks like:
The blade is flat and smooth, usually shaped like a pointed leaf or a kite — wide in the middle and tapering to a point at one end. It is made of steel. The handle is short and fits comfortably in your palm.

What it's used for:
Its main job is to pick up, spread, and smooth soft, paste-like building materials — things like mortar (a paste used to bind bricks together), cement, or plaster (a paste spread on walls to make a smooth surface).

Imagine a bricklayer building a wall. Before placing each brick, they scoop up some mortar with the trowel and spread it onto the top of the previous brick. Then they press the new brick down onto it. The trowel helps them apply just the right amount of mortar and smooth it out neatly. That flat, smooth blade is perfect for spreading soft material the way a butter knife spreads butter on bread — just on a much tougher, heavier scale.

Plasterers use a similar trowel to spread plaster across a wall and then smooth it out to create an even, flat surface. Tile setters use one to apply adhesive before pressing tiles onto floors and walls.

The key action with this type of trowel: spreading and smoothing.

2. The Garden Trowel

This is the trowel used in gardening.

What it looks like:
The blade of a garden trowel is not flat — it is curved inward like a little scoop or a narrow spoon. Think of a tiny, elongated shovel that fits in your hand. The blade is pointed at the tip so it can pierce the soil, and it curves up on the sides so it can hold a little clump of soil or a small plant.

What it's used for:
Its job is to dig small holes, move soil, and plant things. Because it's small and handheld, it gives you much more control than a full-sized spade or shovel.

A gardener uses a garden trowel to dig a small hole in the soil before dropping in a seed or a seedling. They use it to scoop out soil, transfer compost, or uproot a small weed. It is the tool you reach for when you are doing close, careful, small-scale digging — not digging a large pit, but gentle, precise work near plants.

The key action with this type of trowel: scooping and digging.
How to Tell the Two Apart

Masonry TrowelGarden Trowel
Blade shapeFlat, kite/leaf-shapedCurved/scooped, like a small spoon
Used inConstructionGardening
Main actionSpreading paste-like materialsDigging and scooping soil

Even though the two trowels look somewhat different and are used in entirely different fields, what they have in common is this: they are both small, one-handed tools with a blade, designed for precise, controlled work with material — whether that material is mortar/plaster or soil.

When you read or hear the word "trowel" in context, the surrounding words will almost always make it clear which type is meant. "She picked up her trowel and began spreading the plaster" → masonry trowel. "He used a trowel to plant the seedlings" → garden trowel.

• The bricklayer used a trowel to spread mortar before laying each brick.
  • She kept a small trowel in her gardening kit for planting bulbs.
  • He smoothed the wet cement with a trowel until the surface was perfectly even.
  • The gardener dug a hole with her trowel and gently placed the seedling inside.

That's everything you need to know about the noun "trowel." It is a simple, ancient tool — but an essential one in both construction and gardening.
16356:
Truancy is the act of staying away from school without permission and without a good reason. It is what happens when a student who is supposed to be in school deliberately chooses not to go — not because they are sick, not because of a family emergency, but simply because they don't want to attend.

Think of it this way: if you are a student and you are expected at school today, but instead you wander around the park, hang out at a friend's house, or just stay home — without telling anyone or getting approval — that act of deliberate, unauthorized absence is called truancy.

There are two things that must both be true for something to count as truancy:

1. The absence is unauthorized.
This means no one in authority (like a parent, guardian, or school official) has given permission for the student to miss school. If your parent calls the school and says you are unwell, that is an excused absence — not truancy. Truancy only happens when the absence is done without approval.

2. There is no legitimate reason.
Illness, a family bereavement, a genuine emergency — these are valid reasons to miss school. Truancy involves no such valid reason. The student is simply choosing to not be there.

Both conditions matter. An absence that is unauthorized and unjustified is truancy.
A Single Event or a Pattern?

Truancy can refer to:

  • A single act — missing school on one particular day without permission. "His truancy on Friday did not go unnoticed."
  • A repeated habit — a pattern of regularly skipping school. This is often called chronic truancy, and it is treated far more seriously. "Years of truancy had left him far behind his classmates."

When used without any extra description, truancy can mean either, but in serious discussions (legal, educational, or social), it usually implies a recurring pattern rather than a one-off incident.
Who Does the Word Apply To?

Truancy almost always refers to school-age children and teenagers — students who are legally required to attend school. In most countries, education is compulsory up to a certain age (often 16 or 18), which means attending school is not just a personal choice — it is a legal obligation. This legal dimension is what gives truancy its weight and seriousness.

Truancy is not a neutral word. It carries a negative tone. It implies irresponsibility, rule-breaking, and a disregard for one's education. It is associated with:

  • Academic consequences — falling behind in studies, failing exams, or dropping out.
  • Legal consequences — in many places, habitual truancy can result in fines for the student's parents, mandatory counseling, or even court involvement.
  • Social consequences — it is often linked (in research and in public perception) with other risky behaviors, since unsupervised students may fall into harmful company or activities.

So when someone uses the word "truancy," it is not merely describing absence — it is pointing to a problem that has real consequences.

While truancy almost always appears in the context of school, it can occasionally be used more loosely in formal writing to describe any kind of deliberate, unauthorized absence from a place where one's presence is expected or required — such as work or duty. However, this extended usage is uncommon. In everyday life, if you hear or read "truancy," it almost certainly means skipping school.

Here are the closely related words so you have the complete picture:

  • Truancy (noun) — the act or habit itself. "Truancy is a growing problem in urban schools."
  • Truant (noun) — the person who commits truancy; a student who skips school without permission. "He was labeled a truant by the age of twelve."
  • Truant (adjective) — describing someone or something that is absent without permission. "A truant student was found at the mall."
  • To play truant (verb phrase) — the act of skipping school. "She played truant for an entire week." (This is more common in British English.)

• "The school contacted her parents after her third incident of truancy this month."
  • "Truancy rates rose sharply during the economic crisis, as more students were forced to work."
  • "The new counseling program was designed specifically to address truancy among at-risk youth."
  • "His truancy was not laziness — it turned out he was being bullied and feared coming to school."

If you ever need to recall this word quickly: truancy = deliberately skipping school without permission and without a valid reason. It is a problem, it is often illegal for school-age students, and it has real consequences for their lives.
16357:
A truant is a student who deliberately stays away from school without permission and without a valid reason.

The three key parts of this definition all matter equally:

  1. Deliberately — the student chooses to be absent. A truant is not someone who is genuinely sick in bed or dealing with a family emergency. The absence is a choice.
  2. Without permission — the school (and usually the parents) do not know about it, or have not approved it.
  3. Without a valid reason — there is no acceptable excuse. They are simply avoiding school.

So if a student feels like watching TV instead of going to school, slips out of the house without telling their parents, and skips the entire school day — that student is a truant.
What Makes Someone a Truant (and What Doesn't)

This is where many learners get confused, so let's be precise.

A truant IS:

  • A student who skips school on purpose
  • A student who hides their absence from parents and teachers
  • A student who does this with no legitimate excuse

A truant is NOT:

  • A student who is absent because they are sick
  • A student whose parents have told the school they won't be in
  • A student who misses school due to a genuine emergency

The word carries a strong sense of irresponsibility and deliberate avoidance. When you call someone a truant, you are saying they are neglecting something they are obligated to do, and they know it.

"Truant" is not a neutral word. It carries a negative, disapproving tone. It suggests the person is being lazy, careless, or rebellious. Nobody says "what a great truant he is." The word almost always implies mild to serious wrongdoing, depending on the context.
The Related Words You Will Encounter

Since you want a complete understanding, you should also know the words that belong to the same family, as you will almost certainly see them used alongside "truant":

  • Truancy (noun) — this is the behaviour itself, the act of being a truant. Example: "The school has a serious problem with truancy." (Truancy = the problem of students skipping school.)
  • Play truant — this is the most common phrase/verb form. It simply means to act as a truant, i.e., to skip school without permission. Example: "He played truant three times last month."
  • Truant officer — a person employed by a school or local authority whose job is to track down students who are absent without reason and investigate why.

While "truant" most commonly refers to a student skipping school, it can occasionally be used in a broader, more figurative sense to describe anyone who is neglecting a duty or obligation they are expected to fulfill — like an employee who repeatedly disappears from work without reason. However, this broader usage is less common. When you see the word in everyday life, it almost always refers to a school-going student.
Putting It All Together — Examples in Sentences

• "The teacher noticed that Jake had been absent for three days in a row and reported him as a truant." (Jake skipped school without permission.)
  • "Truants often hang around shopping malls and parks during school hours." (Students who have skipped school.)
  • "She was labelled a truant after being caught downtown during class time." (She was caught avoiding school deliberately.)
A truant is a student who deliberately skips school without permission and without any good reason — and the word always carries a tone of disapproval.
16358:
A truce is a mutual, temporary agreement between two opposing sides to stop fighting each other. Both sides agree — at the same time — to pause their conflict for a set period or until a certain condition is met. Neither side wins, neither side surrenders. They simply agree to stop, together, for a while.

Think of it like pressing a "pause button" on a fight — one that both players press at the same time.
Breaking It Down — Three Key Parts

Every truce has three essential qualities. Miss any one of them, and it's not really a truce:

1. It is mutual.
One side alone cannot declare a truce. Both (or all) opposing sides must agree to it. If only one side stops fighting while the other keeps going, that's a surrender or a retreat — not a truce. A truce is always a two-way street.

2. It is temporary.
This is the most important thing to understand about a truce. It is not a permanent end to the conflict. It is a pause — a breathing space. The underlying disagreement or hostility is still there; the two sides have simply agreed not to act on it for now. The fight could resume when the truce ends.

3. It is specific.
A truce usually has a defined purpose or timeframe. It might last for a few hours, a few days, or even years. It is often called for a specific reason — to allow the wounded to be rescued, to let negotiations happen, to observe a religious holiday, or simply to prevent further bloodshed while a longer solution is worked out.

In War and Military Conflict

This is the most classic use of the word. When two armies or two countries are at war and they agree to stop shooting at each other temporarily, that agreement is called a truce.

After weeks of heavy fighting, the two armies agreed to a truce to recover their dead and tend to the wounded.

A famous real-world example is the Christmas Truce of 1914, during World War I, when German and British soldiers spontaneously stopped fighting on Christmas Eve and even played football together in No Man's Land — before the war resumed.

In Politics

The word is used when political rivals or opposing groups agree to stop attacking, criticizing, or undermining each other — at least for a while.

The two political parties declared a truce during the national crisis and agreed to work together.

In Everyday Personal Life

You don't need a war to use this word. In everyday language, a truce is used whenever two people who are arguing or feuding agree to stop — even temporarily.

After days of arguing, the two brothers finally called a truce.
"Truce?" she asked, extending her hand. He shook it. The argument was over — for now.

This informal use is extremely common and completely natural.

Understanding what a truce is not helps sharpen your understanding of what it is:

A truce is not peace.
Peace is a permanent, resolved end to conflict. A truce is temporary. After a truce, a war can — and often does — resume. Peace means the conflict is over. A truce only means the conflict is on hold.

A truce is not a surrender.
When someone surrenders, they admit defeat and submit to the other side. A truce involves no defeat and no submission. Both sides remain equal in status — they have simply chosen to stop fighting for now.

A truce is not a peace treaty.
A peace treaty is a formal, legal, and typically permanent document that ends a conflict and sets terms for the future. A truce is informal by comparison — it is simply a mutual agreement to pause. A peace treaty often follows a truce, but they are not the same thing.
Common Ways This Word Is Used in Sentences

These phrases come up constantly with the word truce:

  • Call a truce — to mutually decide to stop fighting → "Let's call a truce."
  • Declare a truce — to formally announce a stop to fighting
  • Agree to a truce — to accept a pause in conflict
  • Break a truce — to violate the agreement and start fighting again → "He broke the truce by attacking at dawn."
  • Negotiate a truce — to work out the terms of a temporary stop to fighting
  • Reach a truce — to successfully arrive at a mutual agreement to stop
  • Honor a truce — to respect and uphold the agreement
  • An uneasy truce — a truce that feels unstable or fragile, where both sides are suspicious of each other
  • A fragile truce — similar; a truce that could easily break down
The Tone and Feel of the Word

The word "truce" carries a feeling of tension held in check. When you read or hear that two sides have agreed to a truce, you understand that things were bad, that both sides are exhausted or cautious, and that the situation is still unresolved. A truce is not a happy ending — it is more like a cautious pause before the story continues.

It can also carry a feeling of relief — especially in personal contexts. When two friends call a truce after a long argument, there is a sense of both sides being ready to let go of the hostility, even if the issue isn't fully settled.
One Sentence to Remember It By

If you had to remember just one thing about this word, let it be this:

A truce is a temporary, mutual agreement to stop fighting — not because the conflict is over, but because both sides have chosen to pause it.

That single idea captures everything essential about the word truce.
16359:
A truckle is a small wheel or roller — specifically the kind used beneath furniture or objects to make them easy to move. Think of the little wheels attached to the legs of a heavy bed or crate so you can roll it across the floor. Those small, humble wheels are truckles.

The key qualities of a truckle are:

  • It is small (not a grand carriage wheel, but a modest, low-to-the-ground wheel)
  • It is functional (its purpose is to let something roll or move)
  • It is typically set underneath something heavy

The most historically common use of "truckle" as a noun is in the phrase "truckle bed" (sometimes called a trundle bed).

A truckle bed is a low, flat bed fitted with small wheels (truckles) underneath it, designed so that it can be rolled under a taller, larger bed during the day to save space, and pulled out at night for sleeping.

Imagine a master bedroom in a wealthy household centuries ago. The lord or lady of the house slept in a grand, tall four-poster bed. Their servant, however, slept nearby on a much simpler, lower bed — one that could be tucked away out of sight under the big bed each morning. That servant's bed was the truckle bed.

This is why the truckle bed carries a subtle social meaning beyond its physical description: it was associated with a lower-status person who literally slept at a lower level, beneath the grander bed of their superior. The servant who slept on the truckle bed was physically subordinate — and the word absorbed that social flavour over time.

In British English especially, "truckle" also refers to a small, cylindrical (drum-shaped) form of cheese.

If you have ever seen a classic round block of Cheddar or similar hard cheese — the compact, squat, drum-like shape — that is a truckle of cheese. The connection back to the original meaning is the shape: the round, wheel-like form of the cheese resembles a small roller or wheel.

You might hear someone in a British deli say, "I'd like a truckle of Cheddar," meaning one of those neat, small cylindrical cheese rounds, as opposed to a large wheel or a slab. Truckles of cheese are also popular as gifts because of their tidy, self-contained shape.

All three meanings grow from the same seed:

FormWhat it isThe connection
Truckle (basic)A small wheel or rollerThe root meaning
Truckle bedA low bed on small wheelsNamed for the wheels beneath it
Truckle of cheeseA small cylindrical cheeseNamed for its wheel-like shape

Here are some example sentences to cement the meaning:

  • "The heavy wardrobe was fitted with iron truckles so the maids could move it during cleaning."
  • "The young apprentice made his bed on the truckle that slid beneath his master's."
  • "She wrapped the truckle of aged Red Leicester in cloth and placed it in the basket."

It is worth noting that "truckle" also exists as a verb (meaning to submit weakly to someone, to give in servilely), but that is a separate matter from its noun form. As a noun, truckle has nothing to do with submission — it is purely about small wheels and the things shaped like or mounted on them.
A truckle is a small wheel or roller, most commonly encountered in the phrases truckle bed (a low, wheeled bed stored under a larger one) and truckle of cheese (a small, drum-shaped round of cheese).
